questions.q: What are the four steps in the human preference data collection pipeline described in this lesson?
options: Prompt sampled → two completions generated → human picks the better one → pair stored
Prompt sampled → model trains on it → reward computed → policy updated
Human writes a prompt → model is fine-tuned → reward model is discarded
Two humans argue about a prompt → a third human breaks the tie → the loser is deleted
questions.explain: The pipeline is: sample a prompt, generate two (or more) completions for it, have a human annotator pick the better one, and store that choice as a chosen/rejected pair.

questions.q: Why are the two compared completions usually sampled from the model currently being trained (or a close predecessor), rather than from unrelated sources?
options: It is cheaper to generate text that way
It keeps the preference data informative about that specific model's actual tendencies and failure modes, which is what the reward model needs to discriminate during later RL
Unrelated completions are not allowed by the Gymnasium API
It removes the need for a written annotator rubric
questions.explain: On-policy sampling makes the comparisons relevant to the choices the model being trained actually tends to make, which is why preference collection is often an iterative loop alongside training.

questions.q: What fields make up a single stored preference example in the dataset format used later for reward model training?
options: prompt, chosen, rejected
prompt, reward, discount_factor
observation, action, next_observation
username, timestamp, score
questions.explain: A preference pair stores the prompt along with the chosen (preferred) response and the rejected response, which is exactly the shape of data fed into a reward-model trainer.

questions.q: Why do preference-collection pipelines give annotators a written rubric instead of relying on unguided personal taste?
options: Because rubrics are required by law
Because without shared guidance, annotators can disagree inconsistently, so written rubrics and calibration examples improve agreement and consistency across annotators and sessions
Because rubrics eliminate the need to collect any human data
Because unguided taste always produces more data
questions.explain: Shared rubrics and calibration examples help different annotators (and the same annotator across sessions) make more consistent comparative judgments.

questions.q: What does persistently low annotator agreement on a particular category of prompt most likely indicate?
options: The reward model training code has a bug
That category should be removed from the dataset immediately with no further analysis
The rubric may need clarifying for that category, or the prompt may be asking annotators to resolve something genuinely ambiguous
The completions were not sampled from the policy model
questions.explain: Low agreement is itself informative — it often signals an unclear rubric or genuine ambiguity in what 'better' means for that type of prompt, rather than simple annotator error.
